teaser: Open source is a copyright licence, not a free-for-all: six misconceptions corrected, and why the point is that nobody can lock you in.
core_idea: Open source is a copyright licence in which the holder grants copying, use and change; it began as the GPL's copyleft and was reframed pragmatically as open source in 1998; the common misconceptions are that nobody controls it, that anybody contributes, that it is more or less secure than proprietary software, that it costs nothing, that open weights are open source, and that no licence is the most open choice; the security metric is whether somebody had the time and money to review the code; maintainers need funding models; and the real power of open source is that nobody can lock you in and the whole development workflow is yours, which is why there is no sovereignty without it.

nodes.label: Open source is a copyright licence
nodes.summary: The holder uses the right to control copying to grant copying, use and change, on stated terms.

nodes.label: Copyleft made sharing a condition
nodes.summary: The GPL, from Stallman and the FSF in 1989: distribute what you build from it and it carries the same licence; critics called it viral.

nodes.label: Open source, 1998, the pragmatic reframing
nodes.summary: Coined by Christine Peterson; the OSI founded by Perens and Raymond; Linux stayed on GPLv2, its pragmatism was the attitude.

nodes.label: No licence is all rights reserved
nodes.summary: Without a licence ordinary copyright applies and nobody may copy; a permissive licence like Apache 2.0 is what opens it.

nodes.label: A few maintainers control what goes in
nodes.summary: Contributions are reviewed, signed off and refused; the control is real and visible; anybody can fork, nobody can change yours.

nodes.label: Most projects are run by a few people
nodes.summary: The barrier to contributing is lower, and outside a few very popular projects contributions are not the norm.

nodes.label: Security is about time, not openness
nodes.summary: Code somebody had the time and money to review is more secure, open or closed; proprietary products are mostly open source underneath.

nodes.label: Somebody is always paying
nodes.summary: Around 60% of maintainers call themselves unpaid hobbyists; paid maintainers adopt more security practices; a tragedy of the commons.

nodes.label: The xz utils backdoor
nodes.summary: A critical library maintained by one person, an attacker who earned trust over years, found in 2024 because SSH was slow.

nodes.label: Open weights are a compiled binary
nodes.summary: You can run weights, not rebuild them; the OSI's Open Source AI Definition requires code, parameters and data information.

nodes.label: Openness is not the danger
nodes.summary: The question is how tools are used; Metasploit made exploitation easier and the world adjusted; hosting and distribution are themselves control.

nodes.label: The point is that nobody can lock you in
nodes.summary: Read it, run it, fix it, move it, and own the whole development workflow, which survives an acquisition.

nodes.label: No sovereignty without open source
nodes.summary: Sovereignty is the ability to move, and only control that survives a change of owner counts.

quotes.text: The control is real. It is just visible.
quotes.why: The answer to the misconception heard at the event.

quotes.text: For me, the power of open source has nothing to do with the fact that people can contribute.
quotes.why: The point is no lock-in and owning the workflow.
